newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian markets rise further, but caution creeps in.
newsitem.headline: Indian markets rise further, but caution creeps in.

text.p: Indian stockmarkets climbed sharply for the second day on Wednesday in response to the central bank's new credit policy, but some dealers warned the rally could be shortlived.
They pointed to falling industrial production taking its toll on the market, which they said had yet to factor in a slowing economy.
"The industrial scene is bad. Most industrial sectors are not doing well and the market has not taken this into account," said Kamal Kabra, a member broker and former president of the BSE.
"None of the major indications on the economic front have changed. We still see a lot of question marks around," said Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive of Lloyds Securities.
He said the outlook for the stock was cautious. "The 3,350 mark is a level where we have to wait and watch to see if the rally sustains."
The Bombay share index has jumped about 205 points, or 6.5 percent, in the past two days after the central bank eased liquidity and sparked cuts in lending rates at the weekend.
On Wednesday, the Bombay Stock Exchange's (BSE) 30-share index rose 108.23 points, or 3.35 percent, to a provisional 3,335.36.
Buying by local funds and investors has been the major factor spurring market activity, dealers said.
"It is all speculative buying," Kabra said.
"I haven't heard of foreign funds or institutions putting big orders in the market," he said, adding that "a short rally will not take us anywhere".
Analysts said the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy for the first half of the 1996/97 (April-March) financial year came as a shot in the arm.
On Saturday, the central bank slashed the mandatory cash reserve ratios (CRR) of banks by two percentage points to 10 percent, a move aimed at putting pressure on interest rates.
"The good news came at a time when the market did not expect it," said Agarwal. "The rally was fuelled by the CRR cut."
This would help industry tide over a liquidity crunch that has affected companies for over a year, analysts say.
Vikas Saraf, head of research at SSKI Securities said: "I don't see the rally in share prices sustaining for very long".
Despite its market friendly policy, the RBI announcements were not expected to achieve much by way of industrial growth, Saraf said.
The RBI said industrial production, which has been the driving force behind the real growth of gross domestic product in 1995-96, had weakened.
During the first quarter of 1996/97 (April-March), the industrial production index showed 8.5 percent growth, much lower than the 14.7 percent recorded in the first quarter of 1995-96.
Prices of government securities have been firming up even before the policy announcement on expectations of CRR cut. The price rise continued on Wednesday.
